claim: Genetic analyses and systematic mutagenesis have revealed that synonymous, non-synonymous and intronic mutations frequently alter the inclusion levels of alternatively spliced exons.
source: Genetic analyses and systematic mutagenesis have revealed that synonymous, non-synonymous and intronic mutations frequently alter the inclusion levels of alternatively spliced exons, consistent with the concept that altered splicing might be a common mechanism by which mutations cause disease.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior work and is presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: Most exons expressed in any cell are highly-included in mature mRNAs.
source: However, most exons expressed in any cell are highly-included in mature mRNAs.
evidence: This claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A showing the distribution of exon inclusion levels.

claim: Mutations only very rarely alter the inclusion of highly-included exons.
source: Here, by performing deep mutagenesis of highly-included exons and by analysing the association between genome sequence variation and exon inclusion across the transcriptome, we report that mutations only very rarely alter the inclusion of highly-included exons.
evidence: This is the main finding of the study, supported by deep mutagenesis experiments and genetic variation analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mutations that affect splicing are focussed in and around alternatively spliced exons with intermediate inclusion levels.
source: Therefore, mutations that affect splicing are not evenly distributed across primary transcripts but are focussed in and around alternatively spliced exons with intermediate inclusion levels.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the experimental data and analyses presented in the manuscript.

claim: Pre-mRNA splicing is a regulated step in eukaryotic gene expression in which introns are removed from primary transcripts and exons are joined together to form mature mRNAs.
source: Pre-mRNA splicing is a regulated step in eukaryotic gene expression in which introns are removed from primary transcripts and exons are joined together to form mature mRNAs that are subsequently exported to the cytoplasm for translation (Braunschweig et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge in molecular biology, supported by a citation.

claim: Exon-intron boundaries consist of highly-conserved splice site sequences including intronic and exonic nucleotides.
source: These boundaries consist of highly-conserved splice site sequences including intronic and exonic nucleotides.
evidence: This is established knowledge about splice site sequences.

claim: Pre-mRNAs contain exonic and intronic sequences that interact with different splicing factors to regulate how often each exon is included in the final transcript.
source: Apart from the splice sites, pre-mRNAs contain exonic and intronic sequences that interact with different splicing factors to regulate how often each exon is included in the final transcript (Wang and Burge, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior work.

claim: Alterations in splicing contribute to diseases ranging from autoimmune diseases to neurodevelopmental disorders and cancer.
source: Alterations in splicing contribute to diseases ranging from autoimmune diseases (Agrebi et al., 2017) to neurodevelopmental disorders (Xiong et al., 2015) and cancer (Bonnal et al., 2020; Cancer Genome Atlas Research Network et al., 2018; Rahman et al., 2020; Rhine et al., 2018; Supek et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior studies.

claim: In one analysis a third of disease-causing mutations were predicted to result in aberrant splicing.
source: Indeed, in one analysis a third of disease-causing mutations were predicted to result in aberrant splicing (Lim et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: 10% of 4964 disease-causing missense mutations altered the inclusion of cassette exons when tested in an episomal mini-gene construct.
source: and in another 10% of 4964 disease-causing missense mutations altered the inclusion of cassette exons when tested in an episomal mini-gene construct (Soemedi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: 60–70% of all single-nucleotide substitutions alter exon inclusion in FAS exon 6, RON exon 11, and WT1 exon 5.
source: These studies revealed that 60–70% of all single-nucleotide substitutions and mutations in over 90% of exon positions alter exon inclusion (Braun et al., 2018; Julien et al., 2016; Ke et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to deep mutational scanning studies.

claim: Mutations in ~80% of intronic positions flanking RON exon 11 affect its inclusion.
source: One study where the flanking introns were also mutagenized (Braun et al., 2018) further revealed that mutations in ~80% of intronic positions flanking RON exon 11 also affect its inclusion.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a specific study.

claim: Wild-type FAS exon six had a percent spliced in (PSI) of ~50%.
source: in the assayed conditions, wild-type (WT) FAS exon six had a percent spliced in (PSI, the percentage of mature transcripts that include the exon) of ~50%
evidence: This is a specific measurement from a cited study.

claim: RON exon 11 had a PSI of ~60%.
source: RON exon 11 had a PSI of ~60%
evidence: This is a specific measurement from a cited study.

claim: The different versions of WT1 exon five had PSI values ranging between ~0 and~70%.
source: and the different versions of WT1 exon five had PSI values ranging between ~0 and~70%.
evidence: This is a specific measurement from a cited study.

claim: ~60% of exons with a PSI > 10% actually have a PSI > 90%.
source: In contrast, in any given human tissue, most of the expressed exons are highly-included, for example ~60% of exons with a PSI > 10% actually have a PSI > 90% (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in a figure.

claim: The effects of mutations on exon inclusion 'scale' non-monotonically as the inclusion of an exon is increased.
source: This allowed us to quantify how the effect of each of these 12 mutations changes when it is made in different closely-related versions of exon six and revealed that the effects of mutations on exon inclusion 'scale' non-monotonically as the inclusion of an exon is increased.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors, supported by a citation.

claim: As the PSI of an exon increases from 0 to 100%, the effect of a mutation increases to a maximum and then decreases again.
source: Specifically, as the PSI of an exon increases from 0 to 100%, the effect of a mutation increases to a maximum and then decreases again (Figure 1A), consistent with an underlying sigmoidal relationship between an additive trait affected by mutations and the inclusion level (Baeza-Centurion et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a figure and a citation to prior work.

claim: Only 3.6% of exonic mutations in RON exon 11 are predicted to change the inclusion of an exon with 99% PSI by at least 10 PSI units.
source: For example, according to the distribution of mutational effects in RON exon 11, only 3.6% of exonic mutations are predicted to change the inclusion of an exon with 99% PSI by at least 10 PSI units (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a prediction based on rescaling data from the RON exon 11 dataset.

claim: 42.4% of mutations in an exon with a PSI of 50% are predicted to change inclusion by at least 10 PSI units.
source: This compares to 42.4% of mutations in an exon with a PSI of 50% (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is a prediction based on rescaling data.

claim: The ancestral FAS exon six is included in ~96% of mature transcripts in HEK293 cells.
source: First, we quantified the effects of all single-nucleotide changes in the inferred primate ancestor of FAS exon 6, which differs by 11 nucleotide substitutions from the human exon and is included in ~96% of mature transcripts in HEK293 cells (Baeza-Centurion et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a measurement from the authors' experiments, with a citation to prior work.

claim: PSMD14 exon 11 is included at ~98% in HEK293 cells.
source: PSMD14 encodes a subunit of the 26S proteasome with exon 11 included at ~98% in HEK293 cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is a measurement from the authors' experiments.

claim: 91% of mutations in the ancestral FAS exon 6 have an absolute effect <10 PSI units.
source: Indeed, the PSI distributions in both libraries are narrow, with a mode near the WT levels of inclusion and 91% (ancestral FAS exon 6) and 86% (PSMD14 exon 11) of mutations having an absolute effect <10 PSI units (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a result from the deep mutagenesis experiments performed by the authors.

claim: 86% of mutations in PSMD14 exon 11 have an absolute effect <10 PSI units.
source: Indeed, the PSI distributions in both libraries are narrow, with a mode near the WT levels of inclusion and 91% (ancestral FAS exon 6) and 86% (PSMD14 exon 11) of mutations having an absolute effect <10 PSI units (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is a result from the deep mutagenesis experiments performed by the authors.

claim: The distribution of mutational effects in an exon can be reasonably well predicted with data obtained from a completely unrelated exon.
source: This shows that the distribution of mutational effects in an exon can be reasonably well predicted with data obtained from a completely unrelated exon.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the successful prediction of PSI distributions using rescaled data from different exons.

claim: In the Vex-seq library, 55.2% of mutations in exons with intermediate inclusion levels changed inclusion by more than 10 PSI units.
source: In the bins with exons included at intermediate levels, 55.2% (Vex-seq library), 69.2% (SRE library) and 36.2% (SNV library) of mutations changed inclusion levels by more than 10 PSI units (median absolute ΔPSI = 12.3, 18.3 and 7.0).
evidence: This is an analysis of data from the Vex-seq library.

claim: In the SRE library, 69.2% of mutations in exons with intermediate inclusion levels changed inclusion by more than 10 PSI units.
source: In the bins with exons included at intermediate levels, 55.2% (Vex-seq library), 69.2% (SRE library) and 36.2% (SNV library) of mutations changed inclusion levels by more than 10 PSI units (median absolute ΔPSI = 12.3, 18.3 and 7.0).
evidence: This is an analysis of data from the SRE library.

claim: In the SNV library, 36.2% of mutations in exons with intermediate inclusion levels changed inclusion by more than 10 PSI units.
source: In the bins with exons included at intermediate levels, 55.2% (Vex-seq library), 69.2% (SRE library) and 36.2% (SNV library) of mutations changed inclusion levels by more than 10 PSI units (median absolute ΔPSI = 12.3, 18.3 and 7.0).
evidence: This is an analysis of data from the SNV library.

claim: In the Vex-seq library, 2.5% of mutations in the most highly-included exons changed inclusion by over 10 PSI units.
source: In contrast and consistent with the scaling law and the DMS datasets, the distribution of mutational effects in bins containing the most highly-included exons was consistently narrow (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), with 2.5, 14.8, and 0.5% of mutations changing inclusion by over 10 PSI units in the bins containing the most highly-included exons (median absolute ΔPSI = 2.1, 1.7 and 0.7, respectively).
evidence: This is an analysis of data from the Vex-seq library.

claim: In the SRE library, 14.8% of mutations in the most highly-included exons changed inclusion by over 10 PSI units.
source: In contrast and consistent with the scaling law and the DMS datasets, the distribution of mutational effects in bins containing the most highly-included exons was consistently narrow (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), with 2.5, 14.8, and 0.5% of mutations changing inclusion by over 10 PSI units in the bins containing the most highly-included exons (median absolute ΔPSI = 2.1, 1.7 and 0.7, respectively).
evidence: This is an analysis of data from the SRE library.

claim: In the SNV library, 0.5% of mutations in the most highly-included exons changed inclusion by over 10 PSI units.
source: In contrast and consistent with the scaling law and the DMS datasets, the distribution of mutational effects in bins containing the most highly-included exons was consistently narrow (Figure 3B–D, Figure 3—figure supplement 2), with 2.5, 14.8, and 0.5% of mutations changing inclusion by over 10 PSI units in the bins containing the most highly-included exons (median absolute ΔPSI = 2.1, 1.7 and 0.7, respectively).
evidence: This is an analysis of data from the SNV library.

claim: 58.6% of alternative alleles in exons included at intermediate levels had an absolute effect >10 PSI units in GTEx heart tissue.
source: 58.6% of alternative alleles in the 13th bin, corresponding to exons included at intermediate levels, had an absolute effect >10 PSI units.
evidence: This is an analysis of GTEx data for heart tissue.

claim: Only 2.5% of alternative alleles in the most highly-included exons had an effect >10 PSI units in GTEx heart tissue.
source: In contrast and in agreement with the mutagenesis experiments, only 2.5% of alternative alleles had this effect in the 25th bin, which contains the most highly-included exons in the dataset.
evidence: This is an analysis of GTEx data for heart tissue.

claim: Only 28% of exons have an intermediate PSI between 10% and 90% across 30 GTEx tissues.
source: Combining data across 30 GTEx tissues, only 28% of exons have an intermediate PSI between 10% and 90% (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 2, Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an analysis of GTEx data across multiple tissues.

claim: In exons with intermediate PSI, 43% of mutations are predicted to affect splicing by more than 10 PSI units.
source: In these exons, 43% of mutations are predicted to affect splicing by more than 10 PSI units.
evidence: This is a prediction based on rescaling DMS data to genome-wide exon inclusion levels.

claim: 81% of all exonic mutations are predicted to alter inclusion by <10 PSI units.
source: Indeed, in each tissue the predicted distribution of mutational effects is unimodal and centered at zero, with 81% (95% confidence interval 76.6–86.8) of all exonic mutations predicted to alter inclusion by <10 PSI units (79.5%–88.4% of exonic mutations, depending on the tissue, Figure 4—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a prediction based on combining rescaled DMS data with genome-wide exon inclusion levels.

claim: Only 14–17% of common exonic alternative alleles are associated with changes in inclusion greater than 10% in GTEx data.
source: These predictions agree well with the estimated effects of common exonic alternative alleles (GTEx data, black dashed line in Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 4), only 14–17% of which (depending on the tissue) are associated with changes in inclusion greater than 10%.
evidence: This is an analysis of GTEx data.

claim: 30% of flanking intronic mutations are predicted to alter the inclusion level of a 50% included exon by >10 PSI units.
source: Re-scaling these mutational effects predicts that 30% of flanking intronic mutations will alter the inclusion level of a 50% included exon by >10 PSI units.
evidence: This is a prediction based on rescaling the RON exon 11 intronic mutation data.

claim: Only 6.4% of flanking intronic mutations are predicted to alter the inclusion of an exon included at 99% by >10 PSI units.
source: This is in contrast to only 6.4% of mutations in an exon included at 99%.
evidence: This is a prediction based on rescaling the RON exon 11 intronic mutation data.

claim: In the Vex-seq library, 35.6% of intronic mutations in exons with intermediate inclusion levels altered inclusion by >10 PSI units.
source: In the bin with the 20% of exons included at the most intermediate levels, 35.6% (Vex-seq library), 51.9% (SRE library), and 33.5% (SNV library) of mutations altered inclusion by >10 PSI units (median absolute ΔPSI = 6.5, 10.0 and 5.9).
evidence: This is an analysis of intronic mutations in the Vex-seq library.

claim: In the SRE library, 51.9% of intronic mutations in exons with intermediate inclusion levels altered inclusion by >10 PSI units.
source: In the bin with the 20% of exons included at the most intermediate levels, 35.6% (Vex-seq library), 51.9% (SRE library), and 33.5% (SNV library) of mutations altered inclusion by >10 PSI units (median absolute ΔPSI = 6.5, 10.0 and 5.9).
evidence: This is an analysis of intronic mutations in the SRE library.

claim: In the SNV library, 33.5% of intronic mutations in exons with intermediate inclusion levels altered inclusion by >10 PSI units.
source: In the bin with the 20% of exons included at the most intermediate levels, 35.6% (Vex-seq library), 51.9% (SRE library), and 33.5% (SNV library) of mutations altered inclusion by >10 PSI units (median absolute ΔPSI = 6.5, 10.0 and 5.9).
evidence: This is an analysis of intronic mutations in the SNV library.

claim: In the Vex-seq library, only 1.84% of intronic mutations in the most highly-included exons altered inclusion by >10 PSI units.
source: In comparison, only 1.84, 11.1, and 1.44% of mutations had this effect in the bins containing the most highly-included exons (20% most included exons in each dataset – median absolute ΔPSI = 2.1, 2.3, and 0.74, respectively).
evidence: This is an analysis of intronic mutations in the Vex-seq library.

claim: In the SRE library, 11.1% of intronic mutations in the most highly-included exons altered inclusion by >10 PSI units.
source: In comparison, only 1.84, 11.1, and 1.44% of mutations had this effect in the bins containing the most highly-included exons (20% most included exons in each dataset – median absolute ΔPSI = 2.1, 2.3, and 0.74, respectively).
evidence: This is an analysis of intronic mutations in the SRE library.

claim: In the SNV library, 1.44% of intronic mutations in the most highly-included exons altered inclusion by >10 PSI units.
source: In comparison, only 1.84, 11.1, and 1.44% of mutations had this effect in the bins containing the most highly-included exons (20% most included exons in each dataset – median absolute ΔPSI = 2.1, 2.3, and 0.74, respectively).
evidence: This is an analysis of intronic mutations in the SNV library.

claim: 26.5% of common intronic alleles near exons with the most intermediate inclusion levels are associated with a change in inclusion of >10 PSI units in GTEx data.
source: Considering alternative alleles within 50 nucleotides of each exon and all exons in all tissues, 26.5% of common intronic alleles near the exons with the most intermediate inclusion levels are associated with a change in inclusion of >10 PSI units (bin 13 out of 25; median absolute ΔPSI = 4.9)
evidence: This is an analysis of GTEx data for intronic variants.

claim: Only 1.6% of common intronic alleles near the most highly-included exons are associated with a change in inclusion of >10 PSI units in GTEx data.
source: compared to only 1.6% in the most highly-included exons (top bin of 25, median absolute ΔPSI = 0.02; Figure 5E, data split by tissue shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an analysis of GTEx data for intronic variants.

claim: 8.7% of all proximal intronic mutations are predicted to change exon inclusion by more than 10 PSI units.
source: The predicted distributions were similar to the ΔPSI distribution of common intronic alternative alleles: most mutations have little or no impact on exon inclusion and 8.7% of all proximal intronic mutations are predicted to change exon inclusion by more than 10 PSI units, compared to 7–13% of common alternative alleles across human tissues analysed by GTEx.
evidence: This is a prediction based on rescaling the RON exon 11 intronic mutation data to genome-wide exon inclusion levels.

claim: 7–13% of common intronic alternative alleles near exons change inclusion by more than 10 PSI units across human tissues in GTEx.
source: The predicted distributions were similar to the ΔPSI distribution of common intronic alternative alleles: most mutations have little or no impact on exon inclusion and 8.7% of all proximal intronic mutations are predicted to change exon inclusion by more than 10 PSI units, compared to 7–13% of common alternative alleles across human tissues analysed by GTEx.
evidence: This is an analysis of GTEx data for intronic variants.

claim: 21–31% of common alternative alleles near exons with inclusion levels between 10 and 90% affect splicing by at least 10 PSI units.
source: However, focussing on intronic alternative alleles near exons whose inclusion levels range between 10 and 90% reveals that 21–31% (depending on the tissue) of common alternative alleles near these exons affect splicing by at least 10 PSI units.
evidence: This is an analysis of GTEx data for intronic variants near exons with intermediate inclusion levels.

claim: The effect of changing the cell type was strongest in exons included at intermediate levels in the Vex-seq library.
source: Consistent with our results for the effects of cis mutations, the effect of changing the cell type was strongest in exons included at intermediate levels. Minimal effects were observed in highly and lowly included exons (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an analysis of the Vex-seq library data comparing exon inclusion between two cell types.

claim: Candidate skipping-promoting alleles have stronger effects on the inclusion of alternative exons than constitutive exons at the same starting PSI.
source: Candidate skipping-promoting alleles (alternative alleles in the GTEx population associated with lower levels of exon inclusion) have stronger effects on the inclusion of alternative exons. At the same starting PSI, these alternative alleles are associated with a decrease in the inclusion of an alternative exon by ~5 PSI units more than in a constitutive exon (t test p-value<2.2e−16 for exonic alternative alleles, t test p-value < 2.2e−16 for intronic alternative alleles – Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is an analysis of GTEx data comparing effects in constitutive vs. alternative exons.

claim: Constitutive exons have a higher density of exonic splicing enhancers (ESEs) than alternative exons.
source: We downloaded a list of 1182 putative ESE hexamer sequences from Ke et al., 2011 and confirmed that constitutive exons in our dataset have a higher ESE density than alternative exons (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is an analysis of ESE density in constitutive vs. alternative exons, confirming prior findings.

claim: Alternative exons are enriched among exons with the smallest numbers of suboptimal ESEs.
source: Alternative exons were enriched among exons with the smallest numbers of suboptimal ESEs, and this is also true after restricting our analysis to highly-included alternative exons (Figure 7D, Figure 7—figure supplement 8, Figure 7—figure supplement 9).
evidence: This is an analysis of suboptimal ESE density in constitutive vs. alternative exons.

claim: Robust ESEs are over-represented in constitutive exons.
source: Robust ESEs were over-represented in constitutive exons, with the most robust hexamers being almost twice as likely to be found in constitutive as in alternative exons (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is an analysis of ESE robustness in constitutive vs. alternative exons.

claim: Constitutive exons are not more likely than alternative exons to create new ESEs after inactivating an existing ESE.
source: Constitutive exons were not more likely than alternative exons to create new ESEs after inactivating an existing ESE (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is an analysis of cryptic ESE activation in constitutive vs. alternative exons.

claim: All mutations at the invariant dinucleotide intron positions in RON exon 11 are associated with large decreases in splicing efficiency.
source: Consistent with the high conservation of the 'invariant' dinucleotide intron positions, all mutations at these positions are associated with large decreases in splicing efficiency in the RON exon 11 dataset (Figure 8A).
evidence: This is an analysis of the RON exon 11 deep mutagenesis data.

claim: All mutations in the first and last exon bases of RON exon 11 had strong skipping-promoting effects.
source: all mutations in the first and last exon bases of RON exon 11 (Figure 8A) or the ancestral FAS exon 6 (Figures 2C and 8B) had strong skipping-promoting effects
evidence: This is an analysis of deep mutagenesis data for RON exon 11 and ancestral FAS exon 6.

claim: 100% of mutations in the first or last positions of the ancestral FAS exon six had an absolute effect greater than 10 PSI units.
source: (e.g. 100% of mutations in the first or last positions of the ancestral FAS exon six had an absolute effect greater than 10 PSI units, compared with 87.4% in the rest of the exon).
evidence: This is an analysis of deep mutagenesis data for ancestral FAS exon 6.

claim: 100% of invariant dinucleotide mutations in the Vex-seq library in the bin with the highest-included exons had an effect greater than 10 PSI units.
source: Regardless of the starting PSI, mutations in the 'invariant' dinucleotides had stronger effects than mutations elsewhere in an intron (100%, 53.8% and 80% of invariant dinucleotide positions in the bin with the highest- included exons in the Vex-seq, SRE and SNV multiplexed assays, respectively, had an effect greater than 10 PSI units compared with 1.8%, 11.1% and 1.4% in the rest of the intron, Figure 8C–E).
evidence: This is an analysis of splice site mutations in the Vex-seq library.

claim: 53.8% of invariant dinucleotide mutations in the SRE library in the bin with the highest-included exons had an effect greater than 10 PSI units.
source: Regardless of the starting PSI, mutations in the 'invariant' dinucleotides had stronger effects than mutations elsewhere in an intron (100%, 53.8% and 80% of invariant dinucleotide positions in the bin with the highest- included exons in the Vex-seq, SRE and SNV multiplexed assays, respectively, had an effect greater than 10 PSI units compared with 1.8%, 11.1% and 1.4% in the rest of the intron, Figure 8C–E).
evidence: This is an analysis of splice site mutations in the SRE library.

claim: 80% of invariant dinucleotide mutations in the SNV library in the bin with the highest-included exons had an effect greater than 10 PSI units.
source: Regardless of the starting PSI, mutations in the 'invariant' dinucleotides had stronger effects than mutations elsewhere in an intron (100%, 53.8% and 80% of invariant dinucleotide positions in the bin with the highest- included exons in the Vex-seq, SRE and SNV multiplexed assays, respectively, had an effect greater than 10 PSI units compared with 1.8%, 11.1% and 1.4% in the rest of the intron, Figure 8C–E).
evidence: This is an analysis of splice site mutations in the SNV library.

claim: 36.1% of substitutions in the last exonic position in the SNV library in the bin with the highest-included exons altered splicing by more than 10 PSI units.
source: 36.1% (SNV dataset) of substitutions in the last position and 9.5% of substitutions in the first exonic position in the bin with the highest-included exons altered splicing by more than 10 PSI units compared with 0.5% elsewhere in the exon (Figure 8F–G).
evidence: This is an analysis of mutations at the first and last exonic positions in the SNV library.

claim: 9.5% of substitutions in the first exonic position in the SNV library in the bin with the highest-included exons altered splicing by more than 10 PSI units.
source: 36.1% (SNV dataset) of substitutions in the last position and 9.5% of substitutions in the first exonic position in the bin with the highest-included exons altered splicing by more than 10 PSI units compared with 0.5% elsewhere in the exon (Figure 8F–G).
evidence: This is an analysis of mutations at the first and last exonic positions in the SNV library.

claim: The evolution of lower inclusion levels is likely to involve multiple mutations with each of these mutations individually seeming to have no or little effect.
source: The evolution of lower inclusion levels is likely to involve multiple mutations with each of these mutations individually seeming to have no or little effect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the scaling of mutational effects.

claim: A single mutation was never sufficient to decrease the inclusion of the ancestral FAS exon six to the inclusion levels of the human exon.
source: For example, in our recent study a single mutation was never sufficient to decrease the inclusion of the ancestral FAS exon six to the inclusion levels of the human exon.
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors, supported by a citation.

claim: Only 8% of double mutants, 11% of triple mutants and 19% of genotypes containing 10 mutations reached the inclusion levels of the human FAS exon 6.
source: Indeed only 8% of double mutants, 11% of triple mutants and 19% of genotypes containing 10 mutations reached the inclusion levels of the human exon (Baeza-Centurion et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a finding from a previous study by the authors, supported by a citation.

claim: VUS are most likely to alter exon inclusion if they are located in or close to an alternative exon with intermediate levels of inclusion, or in a splice site.
source: Our results suggest that VUS are most likely to alter exon inclusion, and therefore be candidate disease-causing alleles by this mechanism, if they are located in or close to an alternative exon with intermediate levels of inclusion, or in a splice site.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings of the study.

claim: Most mutations in exons and introns will have negligible effects on exon inclusion considering the entire human genome.
source: Thus, considering the entire human genome, most mutations in exons and introns will actually have negligible effects on exon inclusion.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings of the study.
